questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman is admitted with fever and confusion from a urinary tract infection. Her vital signs are: temperature 38.9°C, blood pressure 96/54 mm Hg, pulse 88/min, and respiratory rate 22/min. The team wants to follow her mean arterial pressure (MAP) at the bedside. Using the standard estimate, what is her MAP?
choices: 54 mm Hg
61 mm Hg
68 mm Hg
75 mm Hg
82 mm Hg
questions.explanation: At a normal heart rate, diastole takes about two-thirds of the cycle, so **MAP ≈ diastolic + 1/3 of pulse pressure**. Pulse pressure is 96 − 54 = 42 mm Hg, and one-third of 42 is 14, so MAP ≈ 54 + 14 = **68 mm Hg**. The tempting 75 mm Hg is the simple average of systolic and diastolic pressure; it overestimates MAP because the heart spends more time in diastole than in systole.
questions.explanation_pt: Com frequência cardíaca normal, a diástole ocupa cerca de dois terços do ciclo, então **PAM ≈ diastólica + 1/3 da pressão de pulso**. A pressão de pulso é 96 − 54 = 42 mm Hg, e um terço de 42 é 14, logo PAM ≈ 54 + 14 = **68 mm Hg**. O valor tentador de 75 mm Hg é a média simples entre sistólica e diastólica; ele superestima a PAM porque o coração passa mais tempo em diástole do que em sístole.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man comes for a routine visit. He feels well. His blood pressure is 172/68 mm Hg in both arms, and his pulse is 70/min and regular. There is no heart murmur. Hemoglobin is normal. Echocardiography shows normal valves, a normal aortic root and a normal ejection fraction. Thyroid function is normal. Which change best explains his wide pulse pressure?
choices: Decreased compliance of the aorta and large arteries
Increased resistance of the small arterioles
Increased stroke volume from a high-output state
Decreased compliance of the systemic veins
Increased blood viscosity from a high hematocrit
questions.explanation: With age, the aorta and large arteries become **stiff** (less **compliant**). Each stroke volume then raises systolic pressure more, and the arteries recoil less in diastole, so diastolic pressure falls and **pulse pressure widens**: isolated systolic hypertension of the elderly. Higher arteriolar resistance mainly raises MAP and **diastolic** pressure, so it would not explain a low diastolic pressure. A high-output state is unlikely with a normal pulse, normal thyroid tests and no aortic regurgitation.
questions.explanation_pt: Com a idade, a aorta e as grandes artérias ficam **rígidas** (menos **complacentes**). Cada volume sistólico eleva mais a pressão sistólica, e a retração elástica das artérias na diástole é menor, então a pressão diastólica cai e a **pressão de pulso aumenta**: é a hipertensão sistólica isolada do idoso. O aumento da resistência arteriolar eleva principalmente a PAM e a pressão **diastólica**, portanto não explicaria uma diastólica baixa. Um estado de alto débito é improvável com pulso normal, função tireoidiana normal e sem insuficiência aórtica.

questions.stem: A healthy 34-year-old woman donates her left kidney to her brother. During the operation, the left renal artery and vein are tied off and the kidney is removed. Assume that the resistance of every other vascular bed stays the same. Which statement best describes her total peripheral resistance right after the kidney is removed?
choices: It falls, because the removed bed was in series with the others
It does not change, because each organ regulates its own blood flow
It falls, because the remaining organs now share the cardiac output
It rises, because the removed bed was in series with the others
It rises, because the removed bed was in parallel with the others
questions.explanation: The organ circulations are arranged **in parallel**, and for parallel beds the reciprocals add: 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... Removing one bed removes one term from this sum, so 1/R total gets smaller and **total peripheral resistance rises** a little. The series option is tempting, but in a series circuit removing a segment would **lower** the total, and the kidneys do not lie in series with the other systemic organs.
questions.explanation_pt: As circulações dos órgãos estão dispostas **em paralelo**, e, em leitos paralelos, somam-se os inversos: 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... Retirar um leito remove um termo dessa soma, então 1/R total diminui e a **resistência vascular periférica total aumenta** um pouco. A opção em série é tentadora, mas, em um circuito em série, retirar um segmento **reduziria** o total, e os rins não estão em série com os outros órgãos sistêmicos.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man has dilated cardiomyopathy from heavy alcohol use. His echocardiograms were done 5 years apart. Five years ago, the left ventricular internal radius was 2.5 cm and the wall thickness was 1.0 cm. Today, the radius is 3.5 cm and the wall thickness is 0.7 cm. Peak left ventricular systolic pressure is 120 mm Hg on both dates. How does his peak left ventricular wall stress now compare with 5 years ago?
choices: About one half
Unchanged
About 1.4 times
About 2 times
About 2.8 times
questions.explanation: By the **law of Laplace**, wall stress = (pressure × radius) / (2 × wall thickness). With the same pressure, the ratio of radius to thickness was 2.5/1.0 = 2.5 before and is 3.5/0.7 = 5 now, so wall stress has **doubled**. The tempting 1.4 comes from the change in radius alone (3.5/2.5); it ignores the thinner wall, which raises stress further and increases myocardial oxygen demand.
questions.explanation_pt: Pela **lei de Laplace**, estresse parietal = (pressão × raio) / (2 × espessura da parede). Com a mesma pressão, a razão entre raio e espessura era 2,5/1,0 = 2,5 e agora é 3,5/0,7 = 5, então o estresse parietal **dobrou**. O valor tentador de 1,4 vem apenas da variação do raio (3,5/2,5); ele ignora a parede mais fina, que aumenta ainda mais o estresse e o consumo miocárdico de oxigênio.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man donates about 500 mL of blood. Afterward, he sits up and has a snack. His blood pressure and pulse are almost the same as before the donation. Sympathetic activity has moved stored blood toward his heart and kept his preload close to normal. Which part of the circulation released most of this stored blood?
choices: The aorta and large elastic arteries
The systemic veins and venules
The small arterioles
The systemic capillaries
The pulmonary arteries
questions.explanation: **Systemic veins and venules** are very **compliant**, so they hold about two-thirds of the blood volume at low pressure. Sympathetic **venoconstriction** lowers their capacity and moves this blood back to the heart, which keeps **preload** and stroke volume up after mild blood loss. Arteriolar constriction is also part of the reflex, but arterioles hold very little blood; they raise resistance and protect blood pressure, not volume.
questions.explanation_pt: As **veias e vênulas sistêmicas** são muito **complacentes**, por isso armazenam cerca de dois terços do volume sanguíneo com pressão baixa. A **venoconstrição** simpática reduz sua capacidade e devolve esse sangue ao coração, o que mantém a **pré-carga** e o volume sistólico após uma perda leve de sangue. A constrição arteriolar também faz parte do reflexo, mas as arteríolas contêm muito pouco sangue; elas aumentam a resistência e protegem a pressão arterial, não o volume.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has had sharp chest pain for 2 days. He had a cold 2 weeks ago. The pain is worse when he takes a deep breath. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse is 96/min. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with concave ST elevation in leads I, II, aVL, aVF and V2 to V6. The PR segment is depressed in the same leads. Lead aVR shows ST depression and PR elevation. No other lead shows ST depression. Which diagnosis best fits this ECG?
choices: Acute anterior STEMI from occlusion of the left anterior descending artery
Transient coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina)
Left ventricular aneurysm after an old myocardial infarction
Brugada syndrome
Acute pericarditis
questions.explanation: Inflammation of the pericardium irritates the surface of the whole heart, so the ST elevation is **diffuse** and **concave**, crosses several coronary territories, and comes with **PR depression**; only aVR shows the mirror image. This is **acute pericarditis**, here likely viral. An LAD occlusion is the tempting choice, but its ST elevation is limited to one territory, is often convex, and usually has **reciprocal ST depression** in the inferior leads.
questions.explanation_pt: A inflamação do pericárdio irrita a superfície de todo o coração, então o supradesnivelamento do ST é **difuso** e **côncavo**, atravessa vários territórios coronarianos e vem com **infradesnivelamento do PR**; só aVR mostra a imagem em espelho. Trata-se de **pericardite aguda**, aqui provavelmente viral. A oclusão da artéria descendente anterior (DA) é a opção tentadora, mas seu supradesnivelamento do ST se limita a um território, costuma ser convexo e geralmente tem **infradesnivelamento recíproco do ST** nas derivações inferiores.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has back pain, constipation, thirst and increasing confusion for 3 weeks. He has a normocytic anemia. Laboratory results: calcium 13.8 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), albumin 3.8 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.0), total protein 9.6 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3), creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (normal 0.7-1.3), and PTH 8 pg/mL (normal 10-65). Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike. Which ECG change is most expected from his main electrolyte disorder?
choices: Short QT interval
Long QT interval from a long ST segment
Peaked T waves and a wide QRS complex
Flat T waves with prominent U waves
Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
questions.explanation: This is **multiple myeloma** with **hypercalcemia** (bone resorption, with suppressed PTH). High calcium speeds up ventricular repolarization, which shortens the ST segment and gives a **short QT** interval. A long QT from a long ST segment is the tempting choice, but that is the sign of **hypocalcemia**, the opposite disorder.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **mieloma múltiplo** com **hipercalcemia** (reabsorção óssea, com PTH suprimido). O cálcio alto acelera a repolarização ventricular, o que encurta o segmento ST e causa **QT curto**. O QT longo por alongamento do segmento ST é a opção tentadora, mas esse é o sinal da **hipocalcemia**, o distúrbio oposto.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had increasing shortness of breath for 1 week. Blood pressure is 88/62 mm Hg and pulse is 118/min. Her systolic pressure falls by 18 mm Hg when she breathes in. The jugular veins are distended, and the heart sounds are faint. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low QRS voltage. The height of the QRS complex changes from one beat to the next in a regular, alternating way. Which mechanism best explains this beat-to-beat change in QRS height?
choices: Alternating conduction down the right and left bundle branches
Variable ventricular filling from atrial fibrillation
Swinging of the heart within a large pericardial effusion
Two ventricular foci firing in turn from digoxin toxicity
Movement of the diaphragm with each breath
questions.explanation: Hypotension, distended neck veins, faint heart sounds and **pulsus paradoxus** point to **cardiac tamponade**. In a large **pericardial effusion**, the heart swings back and forth inside the fluid, so its position relative to the chest leads changes with each beat: **electrical alternans**. Respiratory movement is the tempting choice, but it changes QRS height gradually with each breath, over several beats, not on every other beat; the rhythm is sinus, so atrial fibrillation and digoxin-induced bidirectional ventricular tachycardia do not fit.
questions.explanation_pt: Hipotensão, estase jugular, bulhas abafadas e **pulso paradoxal** indicam **tamponamento cardíaco**. Em um grande **derrame pericárdico**, o coração oscila dentro do líquido, então sua posição em relação às derivações precordiais muda a cada batimento: é a **alternância elétrica**. O movimento respiratório é a opção tentadora, mas ele altera a amplitude do QRS de forma gradual a cada respiração, ao longo de vários batimentos, e não a cada batimento alternado; o ritmo é sinusal, então fibrilação atrial e taquicardia ventricular bidirecional por digoxina não se encaixam.
